1. Resource Use Recognition (Mining)
#30 (c) Amax Exploration, Inc.  objected to permits being required for miners.
#32 (d) Phelps Dodge Corporation, Western Exploration Office, Arizona  requested that miners be exempt from ORV regulations.
#36 (e) Colorado Mining Association  objected to permits being required for miners.
#39 (f) Texas Gulf Sulphur  stressed importance of access to Federal lands by miners and requested that mining interests be considered in regulations.
#44 (g) Mine Finders, Inc.  wanted to be able to explore without undue restrictions.
#64 (h) Mining Association of Southern California  objected to permits being required for miners.
#96 (i) International Association of Geophysical Contractors  urged the exemption of geological and geophysical exploration equipment when used for their designed purposes.
#21 (j) Messrs. Brady, Bishop, Dickenson, and Kantor, a group of mineral exploration geologists  felt that minerals exploration should be considered as a vitally necessary exception on all public lands open for mineral entry.
#11 (k) Society of Exploration Geophysicists  urged that geological and geophysical survey equipment be excepted from ORV regulations while being used exclusively for their designed purposes.
#14 (1) Mr. J. M. Reynolds, Member of Governor's Mining Adversary
Board, State of Nevada  urged that ORV regulations take into
consideration four-wheel drive vehicles in field of mining,
prospecting, and ranching.
#46-47 (m) Messrs. R. C. Barkley and R. C. Moores, II, District Geologists, Continental Oil Company  stated that little provision had been made for productive use of vehicles in exploration and development of mineral exploration and mining. 
inplementation of Executive Order 11644 on the grounds that Federal agencies should not decide on their own what public lands should be closed or left open without representation and input from each community involved, and requested more time to allow them to participate in these decisions.
